consensus_summary: The tares are the 'children/sons of the evil one' — counterfeit or false people (often applied as false believers/hypocrites) sown by the devil among the true children of the kingdom, indistinguishable until maturity, left to coexist until the end-of-age harvest, then separated by angels and burned. This is treated as unusually settled because Jesus supplies the interpretation in Matthew 13:36-43; disputes concern only secondary matters (field = world vs. church; pastoral/political applications).
book_summary: The tares are the counterfeit sown among the wheat by the enemy — a weed mimicking the true grain until harvest, then bound in bundles and burned; identified as the children of the wicked one, and distinguished from the chaff of the winnowing imagery. Opposite: wheat.
consensus_core_identification: Tares = children of the evil one: counterfeit/wicked persons sown by the devil among the righteous, coexisting until final judgment and then destroyed.
book_core_identification: Tares = the children of the wicked one: the enemy-sown counterfeit that mimics true wheat until the harvest, when it is gathered and burned.
boundary_disagreement: None of substance. The book's note that tares are 'distinct from the winnowed chaff' is a precision clarifying that the tares symbol should not be conflated with the wheat/chaff imagery of Matthew 3:12 — a distinction Response A actually cites as merely a parallel; this is a terminological clarification, not a change in what the tares refer to.
material_contradiction: None. Both identify the tares as the devil-sown counterfeit persons ('children of the wicked one') destroyed at the end-time harvest.
rationale: The book entry restates the consensus core almost verbatim from the Gospel's own decoding: counterfeit sown by the enemy, mimics the wheat, children of the wicked one, bound and burned at harvest. The consensus responses uniformly give the same identification grounded in Matthew 13:24-30 and 36-43, which are exactly the passages the book prints. The only additional element — distinguishing tares from chaff — refines terminology between two adjacent images rather than altering the referent or its extension. The 'opposite: wheat' pairing matches the consensus wheat/tares contrast. No boundary is moved, no cases are added or excluded.
strongest_objection: One could argue the book's explicit 'distinct from the winnowed chaff' remark and its emphasis on the counterfeit/mimicry theme constitute a refinement, since Response A lists Matthew 3:12 chaff imagery as a parallel basis while the book insists the symbols be kept separate. But this concerns a neighboring symbol's boundary, not the identification of the tares themselves, so it does not rise to REFINED.
